newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl backs off from German jobless cut goal.
newsitem.headline: Kohl backs off from German jobless cut goal.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl backed off on Monday from the goal he set with business and labour early this year to cut Germany's almost four million jobless total in half by the year 2000.
Speaking to a congress of his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party, Kohl said the goal of creating two million new jobs was an ambitious one that many considered unrealistic.
"But I would be satisfied if we could reach two-thirds of that presumed number," he told delegates.
The latest unemployment figures showed 3.991 million people, or 10.4 percent of the workforce, were out of a job in Germany last month.
The goal of two million new jobs seemed overly ambitious even when the government announced it last January after a long meeting Kohl held with employers and trade union leaders.

The accord marked the culmination of three months of national debate triggered by engineering union IG Metall's radical offer of wage moderation in return for the creation of thousands of new jobs -- the "Alliance for Jobs".
Kohl and the employers cooled on the idea last spring and management-labour relations turned sour this autumn as several large companies tried to abruptly impose a cut in sick pay benefits.
A study group sponsored by Kohl's loudest critic within the CDU, Saxony Premier Kurt Biedenkopf, said last week the goal of halving unemployment by the end of the decade was unrealistic.
